m: Published Forbes figure, USD; cross-checked against Forbes Indonesia 50 Richest, Dec 2025 ($4.3B)
did: Holds roughly a tenth of PT Bayan Resources, the East Kalimantan thermal coal miner, through the vehicle PT Sapta Sarana Sejahtera, a position taken years before Bayan listed in Jakarta in August 2008. Forbes identifies her as by far the richest woman in Indonesia.
why: Bayan Tabang concession is shallow, low-strip-ratio coal barged straight down the Mahakam, so its cash cost per tonne sits near the bottom of the seaborne curve. When Newcastle thermal coal went past $400 a tonne in 2022 almost all of that price move dropped through to equity value.
obst: Jakarta January 2022 export ban halted all coal shipments for a month to force domestic market obligation compliance, and ESG divestment had already shut most Western banks out of financing Indonesian thermal coal.
turn: The 2022 energy shock after Russia invasion of Ukraine, which lifted Bayan shares roughly tenfold from their 2020 level.

m: Published Forbes figure in USD; stakes in VietJet Air, HDBank and Sovico Holdings
did: Won an air operator licence in 2007 and flew VietJet first commercial flight in December 2011, building Vietnam first private airline into a carrier with more than a third of the domestic market. Also controls Sovico Holdings and is the largest shareholder of HDBank.
why: She ran the airline as an aircraft finance business as much as a carrier: a 100-plus jet order with Airbus in 2016 was monetised through sale-and-leaseback, so delivery margins and lease income covered the thin ticket yields of a market where most passengers were flying for the first time.
obst: Four years passed between the licence and the first flight because the state carrier duopoly and the aviation regulator slowed approvals; then COVID grounded the fleet in 2020-21 and pushed VietJet to its first annual loss.
turn: The February 2017 Ho Chi Minh City listing of VietJet, which repriced the airline publicly and made her Southeast Asia first self-made female billionaire.

m: Forbes estimate of his Canva stake, USD; Canva last marked around $42B in secondary sales
did: Co-founded Canva in Sydney in 2012 with Melanie Perkins and Cliff Obrecht and built the product as chief product officer, turning a browser drag-and-drop editor into a design tool with over 240 million monthly users and multi-billion-dollar annualised revenue.
why: Canva attacked design from the template end rather than the tool end. Non-designers in marketing, schools and small business never wanted Photoshop layers, they wanted a finished-looking artefact, so a freemium template library with a paid brand kit converted seats that Adobe had never been able to price.
obst: The founders were rejected by more than a hundred investors between 2012 and 2013 while running the predecessor product Fusion Books out of Perth, and had to fund the company from a school yearbook business until Blackbird and Matrix backed the seed.
turn: The 2019 launch of Canva for Enterprise and the shift to team seats, which turned a consumer freemium tool into a business that could carry a multibillion-dollar valuation.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; principally his Rakuten Group holding
did: Quit the Industrial Bank of Japan and launched Rakuten Ichiba in May 1997 with 13 merchants, then bolted a credit card, bank, brokerage and loyalty-point currency onto the marketplace to build Japan largest domestic e-commerce ecosystem.
why: Rakuten never sold the goods itself. It charged shopkeepers a flat monthly fee plus a take rate and gave them their own storefront and customer data, which suited Japan dense small-retailer base and gave Rakuten negative working capital while Amazon was buying inventory.
obst: Rakuten Mobile, launched in 2020 as Japan fourth carrier on a cloud-native network, ran up cumulative losses over one trillion yen and triggered a 2023-24 refinancing scramble that forced dilutive equity raises and the partial listing of Rakuten Bank.
turn: The 2000 JASDAQ listing, whose paper currency funded the acquisition spree - Lycos Japan, DLJdirect SFG, Aozora - that turned a marketplace into a financial group.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; his Rocket Lab USA stake at Nasdaq prices
did: Founded Rocket Lab in New Zealand in 2006 with no engineering degree, reached orbit with the carbon-composite Electron in January 2018, and has since flown it more than 70 times while adding satellite components and the reusable medium-lift Neutron.
why: Electron owned the small dedicated launch slot that SpaceX rideshare could not serve: customers who need a specific orbit and a specific date pay several times the per-kilogram rate. Buying Sinclair, SolAero and Planetary Systems then let Rocket Lab sell the whole satellite, not just the ride.
obst: New Zealand had no space law and no launch industry, so the company had to get a bilateral Technology Safeguards Agreement with Washington and the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act through the NZ Parliament in 2016-17 before it was legal to launch at all.
turn: The January 2018 Still Testing flight, the first orbital launch from a private site, which converted a decade of scepticism into a manifest.

m: Forbes valuation of his controlling stake in unlisted Smilegate Holdings, USD
did: Founded Smilegate in 2002 and shipped the free-to-play shooter CrossFire in 2007, which Tencent took into Chinese internet cafes where it became the highest-grossing PC game in the world for years. Added Lost Ark in 2019 and kept the group private, so he still owns essentially all of it.
why: CrossFire was engineered downward, not upward - low-spec graphics that ran on the ageing PCs in Chinese net cafes, with cosmetic and weapon-rental item sales instead of a box price. Licensing it to Tencent rather than self-publishing traded margin for a distribution base of hundreds of millions.
obst: CrossFire failed in Korea. Domestic publishers passed on it and the local launch went nowhere, leaving the studio dependent on a single foreign licensee in a market where foreign games needed a Chinese partner and an operating licence.
turn: The 2008 Chinese launch under Tencent, which turned a rejected Korean shooter into the largest PC game revenue stream in Asia.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; his holding in Hoa Phat Group listed in Ho Chi Minh City
did: Started a construction-equipment trading company in 1992, moved into steel pipe in 1996, then built Vietnam only fully integrated blast-furnace steelmakers - the Hai Duong complex and the $3.4B Dung Quat plant - to reach roughly 15 million tonnes of capacity and about a third of the domestic long-steel market.
why: Vietnam was importing billets and hot-rolled coil while building at 7 per cent a year. Going upstream to blast furnaces instead of staying an electric-arc rebar roller gave Hoa Phat a cost base that Chinese imports could not undercut once freight and anti-dumping duties were added.
obst: The 2022 steel and coking coal whipsaw pushed Hoa Phat to its first quarterly losses in a decade, several trillion dong in the red, just as the Dung Quat 2 expansion was being committed; his own fortune more than halved that year.
turn: The 2017 decision to build Dung Quat, a capital commitment larger than the company then market value, taken over the objections of investors who wanted dividends.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; largely cash from the 2021 Unity sale plus film residuals and Weta FX equity
did: Built WingNut Films and Weta Digital in Wellington, directed the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit trilogies, and in November 2021 sold Weta Digital tools, pipeline and engineering division to Unity Software for $1.625 billion, keeping the artist-facing studio as Weta FX.
why: He took backend participation and ownership of the effects house rather than only a director fee, so the value of every technical advance - motion capture for Gollum, the Massive crowd system - accrued to an asset he controlled and could eventually sell as software rather than as services.
obst: Miramax wanted Lord of the Rings compressed into two films and pulled support in 1998, leaving him weeks to reset the project elsewhere; a decade later the 2010 actors union dispute over The Hobbit nearly moved the production out of New Zealand entirely.
turn: The November 2021 Unity transaction, which converted two decades of illiquid studio equity into cash.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; Emtek Group holding
did: Founded Elang Mahkota Komputer in 1983 distributing PCs, bought the broadcaster SCTV in 2001 and Indosiar in 2011 to control two of Indonesia biggest free-to-air networks, then pushed Emtek into digital - the Vidio streaming service, the DANA e-wallet and a large pre-IPO position in Bukalapak.
why: Free-to-air television in Indonesia is an oligopoly of licences that cannot be issued again, and Emtek owned two of them. That advertising cash flow funded loss-making digital bets - streaming, payments, e-commerce - that no standalone Indonesian startup could have financed through the 2015-2021 cycle.
obst: The 1998 rupiah collapse destroyed his dollar-priced IT distribution business almost overnight; two decades later Bukalapak, taken public in 2021 in Indonesia largest IPO, lost most of its value and forced heavy writedowns at Emtek.
turn: The 2001 acquisition of SCTV, which swapped a hardware reseller margin for a broadcast licence.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; his stake in the privatised Razer plus Razer Gold and fintech assets
did: A Singapore-trained lawyer who quit corporate practice, co-founded Razer in 2005 around the Boomslang gaming mouse and built it into a peripherals and laptop brand, listed it in Hong Kong in 2017, then took it private in 2022 at HK$2.82 a share with CVC and Lim Kaling.
why: Razer sold identity rather than components. The triple-snake logo, Chroma lighting and the Synapse cloud profile turned a commodity mouse into a subscription-like ecosystem, and the resulting brand pricing power carried into Razer Gold, a prepaid game-credit rail with real float.
obst: The Hong Kong listing was a failure - the stock fell far below its HK$3.88 IPO price and stayed there - and the Razer Phone, launched to make the brand a hardware platform, was discontinued in 2019 after two generations.
turn: The 2022 take-private at a premium to the depressed market price, which reclaimed the equity cheaply from public shareholders.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; his stake in Eco-Shop Marketing on Bursa Malaysia
did: Opened the first Eco-Shop in 2003 in the small Johor town of Jementah, selling everything at a single fixed ringgit price, and scaled it to more than 350 stores before listing on Bursa Malaysia in May 2025 in one of the exchange largest offerings of the year.
why: A single price point removes the shopper price calculation and lets the buyer work backwards: every SKU is sourced to a landed cost that clears the fixed margin. Eco-Shop put those stores in second and third tier towns where rents are a fraction of Klang Valley and there is no organised competitor.
obst: The fixed-price model breaks when input costs move. Rising freight, a weak ringgit and the widened sales and service tax forced the price point up from RM2.40 to RM2.60 in 2024, a change that risked the whole proposition with low-income shoppers.
turn: Creador 2020 private-equity investment, which professionalised the supply chain and set up the 2025 Bursa listing.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; his roughly 31 per cent holding in HYBE, converted from KRW
did: Left JYP, where he had produced g.o.d and Rain, to found Big Hit Entertainment in 2005, created and developed BTS from their 2013 debut, listed the renamed HYBE on the KOSPI in October 2020 and bought Scooter Braun Ithaca Holdings for about $1.05 billion in 2021.
why: He moved the economics off record sales and onto a direct fan platform. Weverse and Weverse Shop capture merchandise, memberships, concert streams and communication from the same fandom the label already owns, so revenue per fan compounds without a distributor or a broadcaster taking a cut.
obst: Big Hit was close to insolvent around 2011-13 and BTS was a last attempt by a small agency with no broadcast leverage; more recently he lost the 2023 takeover battle for SM to Kakao and was indicted in 2025 over pre-IPO share dealings.
turn: BTS 2017 Billboard Top Social Artist win, the moment the group crossed from the Korean market into a global touring and merchandising business.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; family stake in WHA Corporation, converted from THB
did: Co-founded WHA in 2003 building built-to-suit warehouses for manufacturers, then in 2015 reverse-acquired Hemaraj Land and Development for about 43 billion baht, making WHA Thailand largest industrial-estate developer, and added utilities, power joint ventures and industrial parks in Vietnam.
why: WHA does not sell land, it sells a package: serviced industrial plots plus water, power and a ready-built factory inside the Eastern Economic Corridor tax zone. When the China-plus-one shift and the Chinese EV export push arrived, BYD, Great Wall, Changan and Foxconn needed exactly that, at speed.
obst: Her husband and co-founder died in 2012, leaving her to run the company alone, and she then financed the leveraged Hemaraj takeover in 2015 while Thailand economy was stalling under the military government installed by the 2014 coup.
turn: The 2015 Hemaraj acquisition, which converted a warehouse developer into the landlord of Thailand industrial east.

m: Published Forbes figure, USD; his roughly 28 per cent holding in Mercari on the Tokyo Stock Exchange
did: Sold his browser-game studio Unoh to Zynga in 2010, travelled around the world, then founded Mercari in February 2013 and shipped a phone-first consumer-to-consumer marketplace that passed 100 million downloads in Japan and listed on the Tokyo exchange in June 2018.
why: Mercari removed the auction. Japanese sellers on Yahoo Auctions had to set reserves, wait days and arrange payment; Mercari let someone photograph an item, name a price, ship anonymously through a convenience store and get paid by escrow in minutes, which pulled in sellers who had never traded online.
obst: The United States business has never made money, absorbing well over a hundred million dollars a year and forcing repeated restructurings, while the share price roughly halved from its 2021 peak as domestic growth matured.
turn: The June 2018 Tokyo listing, then Japan biggest technology IPO in years, which funded Merpay and the payments push.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; family share of the unlisted Wings Group
did: Took the Surabaya laundry-soap workshop his father founded in 1948 and turned it into Wings Group, a mass-market consumer goods company built on So Klin and Daia detergents and, from 2003, the Mie Sedaap instant noodle brand that took roughly a fifth of Indonesia noodle market.
why: Wings competes on distribution depth and price ladder rather than brand spend. It sells single-use sachets through the warung network into towns where Unilever and Indofood ship in cartons, and it owns its own chemicals, packaging and logistics, so it can undercut and still hold gross margin.
obst: The 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, when the rupiah lost four-fifths of its value against the dollar and imported surfactant and palm-derived inputs repriced overnight; in 2022 Mie Sedaap was pulled from shelves in Hong Kong and Singapore over ethylene oxide residues.
turn: The 2003 launch of Mie Sedaap, the first credible challenger to Indofood Indomie monopoly in four decades.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; stake in Ichitan Group on the SET, converted from THB
did: Created the Oishi Japanese restaurant and green-tea brand from 1999, sold Oishi to Charoen Sirivadhanabhakdi ThaiBev in 2008 for about 3.3 billion baht, waited out his non-compete, then launched the rival ready-to-drink tea brand Ichitan in 2010 and listed it in 2014.
why: He treats bottled tea as a promotions business with a beverage attached. Under-the-cap prize draws with televised million-baht payouts drive trial spikes that a fully automated aseptic bottling line - built to run with a fraction of the labour of a conventional plant - can absorb without losing margin.
obst: The 2014-17 Thai green-tea price war, in which his own former brand under ThaiBev discounted hard and the new sugar-content excise tax landed at the same time, cut Ichitan profits by roughly four fifths and forced him to close the Indonesian joint venture.
turn: Launching Ichitan in 2010 against the brand he had built and sold, using the Oishi proceeds as working capital.

m: Dated list figure in USD, no longer on the 2026 list whose cut-off was $1.0B; cross-checked against his roughly 39 per cent of Shift Up at a KRW 1.87 trillion market cap, about $530M
did: An illustrator and art director who designed characters for NCSoft Blade and Soul, founded Shift Up in 2013, shipped the gacha shooter Goddess of Victory: Nikke in 2022 through Tencent Level Infinite, and the PS5 exclusive Stellar Blade with Sony in 2024. Listed on the KOSPI in July 2024.
why: Nikke monetises character art rather than gameplay depth: a rotating banner of limited-time units, a pity counter that guarantees a pull after a set number of failures, and costume sales aimed at a Japanese male audience willing to spend heavily. Two markets, Japan and Korea, supply most of the revenue.
obst: Korea Fair Trade Commission cracked down on gacha probability disclosure after the 2021 player revolt, forcing published drop rates across the industry, and Shift Up shares fell well below their IPO price once Nikke revenue matured into decline.
turn: The November 2022 Japanese launch of Nikke, which topped the iOS grossing chart and turned a small art-led studio into a listed company.

s: CyberAgent annual securities report shareholder table (IRBank), Mar 2026; TSE market cap Aug 2026
m: Modeled: his 16.61 per cent of CyberAgent applied to a market capitalisation of about 662 billion yen, converted at 159 JPY per USD
did: Founded CyberAgent in March 1998 at 24 as an internet advertising agency, listed it on Mothers in 2000 as Japan youngest listed-company president, then built the Ameba blog platform, the AbemaTV free streaming network with TV Asahi from 2016, and the mobile games studio Cygames.
why: The advertising agency threw off cash that funded consumer bets nobody else would underwrite, and Cygames gacha titles - Granblue Fantasy and Uma Musume Pretty Derby, which has grossed well over a billion dollars - now pay for AbemaTV losses. It is a cross-subsidy structure, not three separate companies.
obst: After the 2000 dot-com crash CyberAgent shares fell about 97 per cent and activist investors including the Murakami Fund pressed him to liquidate the company and return the cash; he bought back shares and refused.
turn: The 2004 launch of Ameba, which converted an ad agency into a media owner with its own audience.

m: Published rich list figure of A$953M converted at about 0.66 USD per AUD, the rate prevailing at publication
did: Melbourne-born mathematician who spent eleven years at Facebook and Meta building the ranking and recommendation infrastructure and the Caffe2 and PyTorch stack, then co-founded Thinking Machines Lab with Mira Murati in February 2025 and helped raise a $2 billion seed round at a roughly $12 billion valuation.
why: Frontier-model founding equity is priced on scarcity of people who have actually trained and served models at Meta scale. A seed round that large buys compute up front, and the founders take a large share of a company that has no product, no revenue and no dilution history.
obst: He walked away from a reported nine-figure Meta retention offer in 2025 and from a decade of vested equity to start a lab with no product, competing for scarce accelerator capacity against incumbents with far larger clusters.
turn: The July 2025 seed round, the largest on record, which repriced his founding stake within months of leaving Meta.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; stake in ViTrox Corporation on Bursa Malaysia, converted from MYR
did: Co-founded ViTrox in Penang in 2000 with a few hundred thousand ringgit and built it into a maker of machine-vision and automated optical and X-ray inspection systems for semiconductor packaging and circuit-board assembly, listed on Bursa in 2005 and exporting to chip assemblers worldwide.
why: Penang was full of multinational back-end assembly plants that bought inspection equipment from Japan, Korea and the United States. Being on the customer doorstep meant ViTrox could co-develop recipes with process engineers and service tools in hours, which is what actually decides equipment qualification.
obst: The company opened in the middle of the 2001 semiconductor collapse with almost no orders, and Malaysian firms had no track record in high-end capital equipment; the 2023-24 chip inventory correction then cut earnings sharply again.
turn: The 2005 MESDAQ listing and the first qualification of ViTrox tools inside a multinational assembly line in Penang.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; stake in Monde Nissin Corporation on the PSE
did: Led Monde Nissin Philippine food business and launched Lucky Me! instant noodles in 1989, which took roughly two thirds of the Philippine noodle market, alongside SkyFlakes and Fita crackers. The group bought Britain Quorn Foods in 2015 and raised about 48.6 billion pesos in the largest PSE IPO ever in June 2021.
why: Lucky Me! was engineered for a peso-a-day market: pancit canton and other Filipino flavours rather than Japanese ramen profiles, a single-serve price point that fits sari-sari store change, and distribution through hundreds of thousands of neighbourhood shops that multinationals never reached directly.
obst: The 2015 Quorn acquisition became the drag: meat-substitute demand in Britain reversed after 2021 and Monde Nissin booked impairments of more than twelve billion pesos, pushing the group to a net loss and roughly halving the share price after its record IPO.
turn: The June 2021 listing, which put a public price on a stake she had held privately for three decades.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; stake in Megawide Construction Corporation on the PSE
did: Co-founded Megawide in 1997 with Michael Cosiquien as a two-man formworks rental outfit with about three million pesos, grew it into one of the country largest contractors, and won the public-private partnership concessions for Mactan-Cebu International Airport Terminal 2 and the Paranaque Integrated Terminal Exchange.
why: Megawide vertically integrated into precast and prefabricated concrete, so it bid construction work at a cost base competitors buying components could not match, then used that contractor margin to fund equity in infrastructure concessions where the returns are annuities rather than one-off build fees.
obst: In 2020-21 the government cancelled the unsolicited Manila airport rehabilitation proposal, COVID cut Mactan-Cebu passenger traffic by more than ninety per cent, and Megawide had to sell its stake in the airport concession to Aboitiz to repair its balance sheet.
turn: The 2014 Mactan-Cebu airport award with GMR, the first time a Philippine contractor became an airport owner-operator.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; stakes in DoubleDragon Properties and Hotel101 Global
did: Opened the first Mang Inasal grilled-chicken restaurant in Iloilo City in 2003 at 26, grew it past 300 branches, and sold 70 per cent to Jollibee in 2010 for three billion pesos and the rest in 2016. Then founded DoubleDragon with Tony Tan Caktiong in 2012, building CityMall and listing Hotel101 on Nasdaq in 2025.
why: Mang Inasal sold unlimited rice with a regional Ilonggo dish at a price point below Jollibee, which made it a threat rather than an imitator - which is exactly why Jollibee paid to buy it. DoubleDragon then repeated the pattern in property: community malls in second-tier cities the big developers ignored.
obst: Mang Inasal outran its own cash - franchising a fresh-grilled format nationwide from Iloilo needed capital he did not have, which is why he sold; later DoubleDragon debt-funded CityMall rollout collided with the 2020 retail shutdown.
turn: The 2010 sale to Jollibee, which handed a 33-year-old provincial restaurateur the equity to become a property developer.

m: Published rich list figure of A$637M converted at about 0.66 USD per AUD, the rate prevailing at publication
did: Wrote Octopus Deploy alone in Brisbane from 2011 as a deployment-automation tool for .NET teams, bootstrapped it to roughly $70 million of annual recurring revenue with no sales force, then took a A$223 million minority investment from Insight Partners in April 2021 at about a $1.1 billion valuation.
why: He sold to developers with a credit card, not to CIOs. A tool that solved a painful, unglamorous problem - repeatable releases to many environments - spread bottom-up inside enterprises, so customer acquisition cost was near zero and he never had to raise money or give up control until the terms were his.
obst: He built it as a side project while employed, in a city with almost no software venture capital, and had to keep the product relevant while Microsoft bundled deployment tooling into Azure DevOps and gave it away free.
turn: The April 2021 Insight Partners round, then the largest single venture cheque written into an Australian software company.

s: SGX market capitalisation of iFAST Corporation, Aug 2026; founder shareholding from company disclosures
m: Modeled: founder stake of roughly 19 per cent applied to a market capitalisation of about S$2.70B, converted at 1.27 SGD per USD; stake percentage is approximate
did: Left the head of research job at Kim Eng Securities and launched Fundsupermart.com in 2000, an online no-load fund distribution platform, then built iFAST Financial as the back-end platform for hundreds of financial advisory firms. Listed on SGX in December 2014 and bought a UK bank in 2022.
why: iFAST is a custody and recordkeeping utility dressed as a fund shop. Advisers, insurers and banks plug into its platform and it earns basis points on assets under administration regardless of which funds are sold, so revenue scales with market levels without the distribution cost of an adviser network.
obst: The 2022 derating, when the shares lost most of their value as the Hong Kong eMPF pension recordkeeping contract ran up front-loaded costs and the newly acquired UK digital bank lost money for successive years.
turn: Winning a share of Hong Kong eMPF platform mandate in 2021, which converted a fund platform into a contracted piece of national pension infrastructure.

s: VietnamNet and Vietnamese market reporting on FPT shareholdings, May 2026
m: Third-party estimate: 117.3 million FPT shares, about 6.89 per cent, valued near VND 8.2 trillion, converted at about 26,000 VND per USD
did: Founded FPT in Hanoi in 1988 with a dozen scientists as a food-processing technology company, then pivoted it into IT distribution and offshore software. FPT Software now exports engineering services with tens of thousands of staff, and FPT added a university and an Nvidia AI data-centre venture in 2024.
why: FPT sold Vietnamese engineering hours into Japan, not the United States. Japanese enterprises needed cheaper offshore capacity but would not accept Indian vendors on language and process grounds, so FPT trained thousands of Japanese-speaking engineers and took work Indian firms could not price for.
obst: The first offshore push in 1999-2000 into Silicon Valley and Bangalore burned most of the company capital and nearly killed FPT Software before it had a single large client; Vietnam was also only just emerging from the US trade embargo.
turn: The early-2000s decision to abandon the American market and rebuild the offshore business around Japanese clients.

m: Published rich list figure of A$470M converted at about 0.66 USD per AUD, the rate prevailing at publication
did: Co-founded HiSmile on the Gold Coast in 2014 with Nik Mirkovic and about twenty thousand dollars, selling peroxide-free teeth-whitening kits direct to consumers, and scaled it past two hundred million dollars of revenue before moving into Boots, Ulta and Walmart shelves.
why: They bought attention rather than distribution. Seeding kits and equity to Kylie Jenner, Conor McGregor and Chris Brown put the product in front of hundreds of millions of followers at a fraction of the cost of a dentist-channel or retail launch, and the direct model kept the whole retail margin.
obst: Apple 2021 App Tracking Transparency change wrecked the Facebook and Instagram targeting the whole model was built on, forcing a rebuild around retail distribution, while Australian regulators scrutinised whitening claims and the peroxide-free positioning.
turn: The 2018 Kylie Jenner post, which took a Gold Coast startup to global demand overnight.

s: GREE Holdings shareholder table (IRBank), Dec 2025; TSE market cap Aug 2026
m: Modeled: 8.33 per cent held directly plus 53.47 per cent through his holding company Sequoia, applied to a market capitalisation of about 75 billion yen, converted at 159 JPY per USD
did: Built the social network GREE alone as a side project in February 2004 while working at Rakuten, spun it out that December, then pivoted it onto feature-phone social games with Tsuri-Star and free-to-play item billing. Forbes called him Japan youngest self-made billionaire in 2011 at about $3.5 billion.
why: GREE monetised before smartphones existed, billing through carrier accounts on Japanese feature phones so payment friction was zero, and ran games as services with virtual items rather than as products. At its peak the model produced among the highest operating profit per employee of any Japanese company.
obst: In May 2012 the Consumer Affairs Agency ruled that kompu gacha - requiring players to collect a complete set of randomised items - breached the premiums and representations law. Billions of dollars of market value evaporated in days and GREE revenue never recovered.
turn: The 2007 shift from a social network to mobile social games, which created the fortune, and the 2012 regulatory ruling, which took most of it back.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; privately held P.J. Lhuillier Group
did: Built the family pawnbroking business into Cebuana Lhuillier, the largest pawnshop and micro-financial network in the Philippines, with roughly three thousand branches doing small gold-backed loans, remittance payout, micro-insurance and micro-savings. Also served as ambassador to Italy and Spain.
why: Pawning gold jewellery is instant, collateralised credit for people no bank will underwrite, and the branch network built to do it is exactly the physical footprint remittance payout needs. Each branch therefore earns twice - loan interest and Western Union payout fees - off one fixed cost.
obst: He was building consumer credit infrastructure in a country where most adults had no bank account and no credit record, under tight Bangko Sentral pawnshop rules; a 2018 breach exposed the records of around 900,000 clients and forced a rebuild of data controls.
turn: The late-1980s decision to layer remittance payout onto the pawnshop branch network, turning dead retail floor space into a payments rail.

s: M3 Inc annual securities report shareholder table (IRBank), Mar 2026; TSE market cap Aug 2026
m: Modeled: his 2.9 per cent of M3 applied to a market capitalisation of about 1.19 trillion yen, converted at 159 JPY per USD
did: A former McKinsey consultant who founded M3 in 2000 inside Sony Communication Network, built m3.com into a portal used by roughly nine in ten licensed Japanese physicians, and sold pharmaceutical companies MR-kun, an e-detailing product that substitutes for expensive medical sales-rep visits.
why: Japanese drugmakers spent enormous sums on medical representatives visiting doctors. M3 owned the doctors attention and sold it back at a fraction of the cost per contact, so every rep a client cut became M3 revenue. Once most physicians were on the platform, no rival could assemble the same audience.
obst: Japan pharmaceutical industry was built on face-to-face relationships and was slow to accept digital detailing; after the pandemic pulled forward years of adoption, the reversal was brutal and M3 shares fell roughly three quarters from their 2021 peak.
turn: The 2004 launch of MR-kun, which turned a doctors portal with no revenue model into a substitute for pharma field sales.

m: Published national rich list figure in USD; family stake in RFM Corporation and the Unilever ice-cream joint venture
did: Ran the family company Republic Flour Mills from the 1990s and turned a commodity miller into a branded foods business - Selecta ice cream, White King, Fiesta, Sunkist - then sold half of Selecta into a 1999 joint venture with Unilever that became the Philippine market leader. Founded Go Negosyo in 2005.
why: Flour milling is a spread business with no pricing power. Putting the same wheat and dairy inputs behind brands, then handing the ice-cream brand to Unilever in exchange for half of a much larger business, converted low-margin tonnage into a share of a category with cold-chain barriers to entry.
obst: The 1997 Asian financial crisis and the peso collapse left RFM carrying dollar debt against peso revenue; the group had to sell Cosmos Bottling, its soft-drinks arm, to Coca-Cola and San Miguel in 2001 to repair the balance sheet.
turn: The 1999 Unilever ice-cream joint venture, which traded control of the group best brand for scale and capital at the bottom of the crisis.

s: JYP Entertainment KOSDAQ market capitalisation, mid-2026; founder shareholding from company filings
m: Modeled: his 15.37 per cent of JYP Entertainment applied to a market capitalisation of about $1.19B, plus producing royalties; excludes private assets
did: A singer and producer who founded JYP Entertainment in 1997 and built the Korean in-house trainee and producing model, creating g.o.d, Rain, the Wonder Girls, 2PM, TWICE, Stray Kids and ITZY, plus the NiziU joint venture with Sony Music in Japan.
why: JYP industrialised artist development: multi-year trainee contracts, in-house songwriting and choreography, and long revenue-share terms, so a single hit group amortises the cost of the ones that fail. Localising the model into Japan with NiziU cloned the factory rather than exporting a finished act.
obst: The 2009-12 American push with the Wonder Girls consumed years and money for a single Hot 100 entry and ended with the group breaking up; more recently JYP shares roughly halved after 2023 as China restrictions and normalising album sales hit the sector.
turn: The 2015 debut of TWICE, which restored JYP to the front rank after the failed US expansion.

s: COLOPL Inc annual securities report shareholder table (IRBank), Mar 2026; TSE market cap Aug 2026
m: Modeled: his 48.06 per cent of COLOPL applied to a market capitalisation of about 57 billion yen, converted at 159 JPY per USD
did: Started the location-based game Colony na Seikatsu as a personal hobby project in 2003 while working as an engineer, incorporated COLOPL in 2008, listed it in 2012, and in 2014 shipped Shironeko Project, a one-thumb action RPG with gacha monetisation that became one of Japan top-grossing mobile titles.
why: Shironeko Project was built for the commute: playable with one thumb on a crowded train, with character banners and limited-time events that convert a few per cent of players into very heavy spenders. Japanese mobile gacha revenue concentrates in whales, so average revenue per user is a misleading measure.
obst: Nintendo sued COLOPL in January 2018 over five patents including the touch-and-drag control at the heart of Shironeko Project; the case settled in 2021 with a 3.3 billion yen payment and a licence, arriving as the game revenue was already falling, and the shares are down roughly ninety per cent from their peak.
turn: The July 2014 launch of Shironeko Project, which took the company from a location-game curiosity to a top-ten grossing publisher.

m: The list values her and her husband Dean Steingold jointly at A$486M; halved to her share and converted at about 0.66 USD per AUD
did: A clinical nutritionist who built an audience from 2014 through a blog, books and Instagram, then launched JSHealth Vitamins in 2018 with her husband Dean Steingold. The Hair and Energy formula was the breakout product and the brand scaled past a hundred million dollars of revenue into Priceline and Boots.
why: She owned the audience before she owned a product. Years of free nutrition content meant the launch converted an existing following at near-zero acquisition cost, and a deliberately short SKU range - a handful of formulas rather than a wall of them - kept manufacturing runs long and working capital light.
obst: Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration rules sharply restrict what a supplement may claim, so the brand had to grow on organic content instead of efficacy advertising; the 2022-23 collapse of Instagram organic reach then forced a rebuild of acquisition around TikTok and retail.
turn: The 2018 launch of the Hair and Energy vitamin, which turned a personal-brand nutrition practice into a product company.

m: Published rich list figure of A$220M converted at about 0.66 USD per AUD, the rate prevailing at publication
did: Ukrainian-born former Bain consultant who founded Lyka in 2018, a subscription service delivering gently cooked fresh dog food made in the company own kitchens, and grew it past a hundred million dollars of revenue. She was the highest-ranked female debutant on the 2025 AFR Young Rich List.
why: Subscription pet food is a recurring-revenue business with unusually low churn, because the customer is buying for an animal with a fixed diet and no opinion about switching. Owning manufacturing and the frozen delivery network meant Lyka controlled the cold chain that kept incumbents out of the category.
obst: Roughly nine in ten Australian dogs eat shelf-stable kibble, so she had to build a factory and a frozen last-mile network from scratch to sell a product that costs several times more per meal - and raise the capital for it as venture funding tightened in 2022.
turn: Bringing manufacturing in-house around 2021, which fixed the unit economics that outsourced production had made impossible.
